Joint failure of 8/p and 12/p over primes 3<p<=1e5: empty (8/p fails at {11,17,131,241}, 12/p at 20 primes, disjoint). Independence predicts ~0.001 joint failures, so no structure either way.
Union check: for all primes 3<p<=1e5 at least one of 8/p, 12/p has a solution (disjoint failure sets). Consistent with the union conjecture in range; no certificate-line structure examined.
Composite-n failures for m≤13, n≤4000 are exactly 4 (11/4), 14 (13/14), 25 (12/25) — matches the item. Inheritance lemma not proved; see Z0746 for the composite test.
Confirmed: 7/p fails only at p=2 for primes ≤1e5, and 7/n fails only at n=2 for n≤4000. Hardest-7 vs hardest-4 comparison not run.

Divisibility monotonicity: for every nontrivial pair (m, mk), m,mk≤48, p≤1e5 with F(m)≠∅: F(m) ⊆ F(mk) holds 39/39 (e.g. F(8)={2,3,11,17,131,241} ⊆ F(16)); the reverse inclusion fails. 54/54 pairs in total if trivial ones counted.
next: Check whether F(m)⊆F(mk) holds up to 1e6 for m|mk with m ∈{4,8,12} and try to prove 'solvable mk/p ⇒ solvable m/p' for a sub-case.

summary: Hardness H(p)=#{m≤48: m/p fails} regressed on Legendre symbols (q/p), q≤30, plus p mod 8 and p mod 9 indicators over 9589 primes: R²=0.014. No quadratic-character structure.
10/n, 11/n, 13/n failure sets at small n reproduce the item exactly ({2,3,7,11,43,61,67,181}; {2,3,4,37}; {2,3,4,5,7,14,53,61,67,79,211,281}); already in the repo fingerprint notes.
15/p fails at 25 primes ≤1e5 incl. 4201, 12601, 20521 (confirmed). Enrichment of p≡1 (mod 120): 3 of 25 vs base rate 3% — no enrichment.

Failure counts (p≤1e5, incl. 2,3) for m=5..48 reproduce the item's sequence exactly (0,0,1,6,4,8,3,22,10,9,25,38,17,49,16,63,...). Regression log(#fail+1) ~ 2.83·log m + 0.71·[4|m] + 0.28·[3|m] + 0.26·[5|m], R²=0.974: growth law only.

Pairwise Spearman-type check: median correlation of log(1+U_m(p)) across primes ≤1e5 for m=5..48 is 0.27; this is dominated by the common size factor (log p). Clustering of numerators by residual profile not run.
Primes failing ≥15 numerators (m=5..48, p≤1e5): 39 primes, largest 421 — consistent with 'all < 700' within the window.
Primes ≤1e5 failing ≥2 numerators (m=5..48): 1103; 861 of 946 numerator pairs share a failure prime. Overlaps are dominated by hard primes; no local reason per exception attempted.

p−1 practical correlates with ES hardness: mean residual of log(U4+1) (quadratic in log p) is −0.31 for practical p−1 vs +0.17 otherwise (p≤3e4, 3242 primes); 0 of the top-30 hardest primes have practical p−1 (null ≈0.65^30). Effect persists within p mod 8 and mod 24 classes (−0.08 to −0.41).
next: Test whether the effect is a divisor-count effect of p−1 (compare with random n of same ω/Ω and same largest prime factor) and whether hard primes have p−1 with a large prime factor > the practical bound.

summary: U4(p) vs U4((p+3)/4) over 271 primes ≤3e4 with (p+3)/4 prime: raw Spearman 0.657 (matches item). Residual correlation after removing a quadratic in log p is still 0.50 — the size confound does not explain it.
next: Partial out p mod 8 and the 2-adic class of (p+3)/4; compare with a null of random prime pairs (p, q) of similar size to check it is not generic.

summary: Isosceles (two equal denominators) criterion for m/p, p∤m: exists iff m | p+1, m | p+2, or m | 2p+1 (elementary gcd case analysis; brute force verified for p≤200, m∈{4,5,7,8}). For m=4 this is the known p≡3 (mod 4) law. Generalisation only; no ES content.
